newsitem.title: USA: Motorola stock rises, recovery seen underway.
newsitem.headline: Motorola stock rises, recovery seen underway.

text.p: Motorola Inc. stock rose in active trading Wednesday, a day after the technology giant beat second-quarter earnings estimates and posted growth in orders in its key businesses.
"It's a confirmation that the earnings recovery that everyone on Wall Street has been forecasting is getting under way," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman.
Motorola's stock rose $4 to $86.50 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the second most active issue at midday.

Investors were upbeat even though Motorola on Wednesday lowered its annual growth forecast for the worldwide computer chip industry in 1997 to a range of about 6 percent to 8 percent instead of 10 percent previously.

After the market closed Tuesday, Motorola reported second-quarter earnings of 62 cents a share, excluding a $170 million one-time charge to phase out its struggling dynamic random access memory (DRAM) business.
The result was far better than the 56 cents-a-share consensus estimate on Wall Street.
Including the charge, the Schaumburg, Ill.-based company's profits fell to $268 million from $326 million last year.
Orders in Motorola's two main segments, semiconductors and cellular products, rose 36 percent and 20 percent, respectively.
Lehman Brothers said Motorola was "on the road to recovery". It raised its earnings estimates for Motorola to $2.71 from $2.58 for 1977, and to $3.65 from $3.40 for 1988.
A cyclical downturn in the world semiconductor industry and stiff competition in cellular phones had plagued Motorola.

In a conference call with analysts Wednesday, Ed Gams, head of Motorola investor relations, said industry growth this year is expected to be strongest in the United States and certain Asian regions but smaller in Japan, where demand is hurt by the strong U.S. dollar.
Gam also said Motorola expects to record an expense of about $65 million in 1997 for its share of net losses this year by satellite consortium Iridium LLC.
Motorola has a stake of about 21 percent in Iridium, which plans a global satellite-based telecommunications network. Its stake has dropped from 24 percent as other investors entered the consortium.
The expense is due largely to depreciation of launched satellites and will be taken mostly in the second half of the year, Gam said.

He said Motorola's share of losses from Iridium is expected to be "several times greater" than the $65 million this year, but the losses will have petered out in 1999 as the company writes down its equity investment in the consortium.
